Food for thought

This move was likely at/near its top regardless-- the normal signs started to flash with the leaders rolling over, alt OI and volume dominance-- but we added a "new" FUD which accelerated into a forceful move down

It isn't really new, we knew to be aware of this back before Mythos/Fable class model. What we didn't know is how long it would take to materialize as fear in market participants holding a significant percent of their portfolios onchain/in cryptoassets. Fair to say there's a fatter left tail and more of a chance of it materializing sooner than we thought. 

People instinctively want to label the market as a "bull" or "bear" but it's long been a dispersion market regardless. Even if we are in a "bull" for real money-generating protocols, there's going to be some dead periods and wild 2way vol. I'm going to continue to focus on medium/higher timeframe swings where many liquid 2-6x's have been available with an overall lower % of portfolio. 

Hard to overstate how much better you can sleep with the safety/security of TradFi for the vast majority of portfolio.

Today I call upon the automobile industry to calmly begin planning for "walking mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of commuters to their own feet, i.e. vehicles whose fuel remains hidden behind a hamstring.

Drivers, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their errands to legs that have never touched a gas pedal. And when they do refuel, they should also move remaining gasoline to a new jerrycan (possibly purchased from the same gas station).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Walking is a simple, preventative step which does not require new chemistry or new cars.
IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that gasoline becomes remotely detonatable before peak oil, in the worst case in months not years. By "detonatable" I mean simultaneous ignition of every gallon on Earth (e.g. one Tuesday afternoon) using available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster and a sufficiently clever text message).

Recent days have been humbling for human chemical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. Neither is about gasoline, which is exactly what worries me. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that chemical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of combustion research happen. Could our magic 87-octane fuel be too good to be true? Was it just safety through obscurity all this time?

Hydrocarbons feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Octane carries rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like carbon chains, branching, double bonds. (By contrast, legs are designed to minimise octane rating.)

Separately, as anyone who has seen a Michael Bay movie can attest, a small spark sometimes foreshadows a very large explosion. We should be open to the possibility of a wireless counterpart to the spark plug that ignites every fuel tank and every Zippo at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of universal remote gasoline detonation among the 722 results OpenAI published. The number is zero. Not one AI lab has published a paper ruling it out either. I've witnessed first-hand gas station attendants refusing to answer my questions on this. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. GasBuddy is a great tracker of exposed gasoline. Exxon, Shell, Aramco, Chevron, and your local Wawa have an opportunity to harden their tanks. Tesla appears to have quietly migrated already, which is interesting timing. Next month I'll address institutions in Houston in a live Q&A (attending remotely, on foot).

Again, please do not rush. Cars holding under half a tank enjoy partial cover from "Exxon's shield", i.e. its refineries holding millions of barrels each. Load-bearing drivers like ambulances and ice cream trucks should consider rotating gas stations with every fill-up and/or multi-propelling with a pedal-based scheme like the bicycle.
Exiting walking mode safely will require post-AI propulsion. My inclination is to go all-in on leg-based transportation and avoid structured chemical assumptions entirely, whether from gasoline, diesel, or lithium. A single battle-tested leg (e.g. from the LEFT or RIGHT families) yields plausible post-AI mobility.

The Amish roadmap fully embraces horse-based transportation with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the combustion threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of chemical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

Smart contracts have been live on Ethereum for 11 years.

& on their own, they still can't read a webpage.

Everything they know has to be fed to them as a clean number. Prices. Timestamps. Balances.

The real world is messier. News articles, PDFs, agreements written in English, two sources that disagree.

That's the gap @GenLayer built Intelligent Contracts for.

𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐝𝐨

• fetch & read live web pages
• process text, PDFs & images
• follow rules written in plain English
• use AI to judge outcomes that aren't a simple yes or no
• settle the result on-chain

𝐡𝐨𝐰 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐲 𝐡𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐭

• 5 random validators check each result
• each one runs a different model or config
• majority rules
• appeal it & the panel jumps to 11, then 23, then 47
• around 30 minutes in the normal case

The clever bit: two answers can be worded differently & still count as the same answer. The developer decides what "equivalent" means. That's how a group of different AIs reach agreement.

• marketing deals where brands only pay for real results
• oracles that settle questions instead of trusting one data provider

The agents are coming either way. They'll need contracts that can read.

The market is selling off on “news” that is barely news.

OpenAI reportedly told investors that its annualized revenue was approaching $50B at the end of September, rather than the ~$70B figure that was widely reported last month.

But the gap largely comes down to accounting methodology, not a $20B hole in OpenAI’s business.

Anthropic counts revenue generated through cloud partners such as AWS and Google Cloud, while OpenAI apparently does not. Investors had therefore adjusted OpenAI’s reported figures to make them comparable with Anthropic’s, which helped produce the ~$70B estimate.

So we are essentially talking about whether revenue flowing through cloud partners is included in the headline number or not.

That is a comparability issue, not some sudden collapse in OpenAI’s revenue trajectory.

The fact that the market is treating this as a major negative for AI is, frankly, pretty ridiculous.

Over long periods of time, debts tend to rise faster than incomes, creating the long-term debt cycle.

Even as people become more indebted, lenders freely extend credit because during economic booms, incomes rise, asset values soar, and the stock market thrives. People borrow more to buy financial assets, pushing prices higher and creating a bubble.

So long as incomes keep rising, the debt burden stays manageable. But this cannot continue forever. Over decades, debt burdens slowly accumulate until debt repayments grow faster than incomes. This forces people to cut back on spending, causing incomes to fall and borrowing to dry up—eventually reversing the entire cycle.

“There's been a tremendous amount of economic data in just the last week or two showing that the economy is much stronger than people are giving it credit for.
